Women of Scripture
WIM-en uv SKRIP-chur
noun phrase (biblical-theological category)
From Old English wifman (woman, literally “wife-person,” from wif, woman, + man, person) + Latin scriptura (writing, from scribere, to write; in ecclesiastical Latin, the Holy Scriptures). The phrase denotes the women whose lives, words, and roles are recorded in the canonical sixty-six-book Bible — from Eve and Sarah through Mary Magdalene and Priscilla — as studied in their textual, historical, and theological significance for biblical anthropology, the theology of womanhood, and the history of redemption.

Biblical Definition

Women occupy a prominent and theologically intentional role throughout biblical history. The canon opens with the creation of the woman as a fitting helper (ezer kenegdo) for the man (Gen 2:18–24) — a helper not in the sense of a subordinate assistant but in the sense of the God-given complement who completes what is lacking, a word the Old Testament also applies to God himself as Israel's help (Ps 121:2). Eve is the mother of all living (Gen 3:20) and the first recipient of the protoevangelion’s promise (Gen 3:15). The Old Testament honors women as matriarchs (Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah), deliverers (Rahab, Deborah, Jael, Esther), prophets (Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, Anna), and exemplars of wisdom and virtue (Abigail, the Prov 31 woman, Ruth). The New Testament advances this theology: women were the last at the cross (Mark 15:40–41), the first at the tomb (John 20:1), and the first heralds of the resurrection (John 20:18 — Mary Magdalene's “I have seen the Lord”). The early church was served by women of significant ministry: Phoebe, a deaconess of Cenchrea (Rom 16:1); Priscilla, who instructed Apollos (Acts 18:26); the four daughters of Philip who prophesied (Acts 21:9); Lois and Eunice who passed faith to Timothy (2 Tim 1:5). The complementarian reading of this data recognizes the full spiritual equality and dignity of women (Gal 3:28) while maintaining the gender-differentiated role structure in marriage and church governance that Scripture commends. The full complement of feminine contribution — prophetic witness, hospitality, service, theological instruction, martyrdom, and the faith-formation of households — is not diminished by complementarian convictions but honored within them.

Webster 1828 Definition

The women whose lives and roles are recorded in the sixty-six-book biblical canon — from the helper-complement of Genesis 2 through the first resurrection witnesses of the Gospels and the deaconesses and church-workers of the apostolic letters — honored for their spiritual equality and complementary role within God's ordered design for humanity.

WOMEN OF SCRIPTURE, n. The women whose faith, ministry, and witness are recorded in the canonical sixty-six books — matriarchs (Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel), prophetesses (Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, Anna), exemplars of virtue (Abigail, Ruth, Esther, the Prov 31 woman), and apostolic co-laborers (Mary Magdalene, Phoebe, Priscilla, Lois, Eunice).

2. GENESIS 2 GROUND: woman created as ezer kenegdo (Gen 2:18) — a strength-matching complement, not a diminished dependent; a helper in the sense God himself is called Israel's help (Ps 121:2). Complementarian anthropology begins here, not in hierarchy as domination but in difference as design.

3. RESURRECTION WITNESSES: women were the first to see the risen Lord (John 20:1–18; Matt 28:1–10); Mary Magdalene was commissioned by Christ himself to announce the resurrection to the apostles — making women the first evangelists of the resurrection even while the apostolic office remained male.

4. APOSTOLIC-ERA MINISTRY: Phoebe (diakonos, Rom 16:1), Priscilla (catechist of Apollos, Acts 18:26), Lydia (house-church host, Acts 16:14–15), Lois and Eunice (transmitters of faith to Timothy, 2 Tim 1:5) — a rich picture of women's integral contribution to the early church's ministry.

5. GALATIANS 3:28: “there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” — the ontological and soteriological equality of men and women before God, the ground of women's full spiritual dignity; not the abolition of role-differentiation in marriage and church governance, which Paul maintains alongside this text.

Key Scripture

Prov 31:10 — "Who can find a virtuous wife? For her worth is far above rubies."

John 20:18 — "Mary Magdalene came and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord!” — and that He had said these things to her."

Rom 16:1 — "I commend to you our sister Phoebe — who is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea —"

Heb 12:14 — "Pursue peace with all men — and the sanctification without which no one will see the Lord."

Modern Corruption

The egalitarian movement reads the prominence of women in Scripture as evidence that New Testament role distinctions were purely cultural accommodations to first-century patriarchy, now to be transcended in an equalizing ministry in which gender distinctions have no bearing on office or authority.

expand to see more

The egalitarian reading of women in Scripture collapses two distinct biblical categories: gifting (which the Spirit distributes to both men and women, 1 Cor 12:7; Acts 2:17) and office (which Paul restricts to qualified men in 1 Tim 2:12–3:7; Titus 1:5–9). The egalitarian argues that because women prophesied (Acts 21:9), taught (Acts 18:26), and led households (Acts 16:14–15), the restriction of the elder/overseer office to men must be culturally conditioned rather than creation-grounded. But Paul himself grounds the teaching restriction in Adam's priority in creation (“for Adam was formed first,” 1 Tim 2:13) — a ground that predates culture and persists through all cultural change.

The complementarian position is not that women lack gifts, intelligence, spiritual authority, or theological contribution — the canon's own record refutes any such diminishment. It is that God has designed gender-differentiated roles in marriage (Eph 5:22–33) and church governance (1 Tim 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9) that honor both sexes by giving each their distinctive calling. The full dignity of women in Scripture is best served not by erasing distinctions but by honoring them: the Proverbs 31 woman is not a lesser figure for being a wife and mother rather than a ruling elder — she is among the most celebrated figures in the canon.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew ishshah (woman, from ish, man, by gender-differentiation) and Greek gunē (woman, wife) provide the linguistic range across the two testaments, with the theological concept of the ezer (helper-complement) anchoring the creation-theology of womanhood.

expand to see more

Hebrew ezer kenegdo — a helper as opposite/equal to him (Gen 2:18); the compound term describing woman's complementary-completing function — ezer (helper-strength, used of God in Ps 121:2) + kenegdo (as over against him, a matching counterpart)

Hebrew ishshah — woman, from ish (man); the wordplay of Gen 2:23 (“she shall be called Woman because she was taken out of Man”) grounds sexual differentiation in creation act, not cultural convention

Greek gunē — woman, wife; Paul's standard term in both the equality text (Gal 3:28) and the role-differentiation texts (1 Cor 14:34–35; 1 Tim 2:12) — the same word, same context, two aspects of one biblical anthropology

Greek diakonos — servant, deacon; applied to Phoebe in Rom 16:1 in the same word Paul uses for church officers (Phil 1:1; 1 Tim 3:8–13) — a debated text but evidence of women's formal recognized service in the apostolic church

Reformed complementarianism: spiritual equality (Gal 3:28) + role differentiation (1 Tim 2:12–13; Eph 5:22–33) are both creation-grounded realities, not contradictions; the Confession (WCF/1689) upholds both

Usage

"Deborah's judgeship (Judges 4–5) is often cited by egalitarians as evidence that women may lead in all capacities; the complementarian response notes that Deborah's rise to prominence reflected Israel's spiritual dysfunction (Barak's refusal to lead without her escort brought him the reproach of Judges 4:9) rather than the normative pattern of leadership that Titus 1 and 1 Timothy 3 prescribe for the new covenant church."

"Mary Magdalene as the “apostle to the apostles” (a title used by Hippolytus, c. 170 AD) captures the paradox: Christ chose a woman as the first herald of the resurrection to the Twelve — a sign of the Spirit's equalizing witness — while the Twelve (all male) remained the authoritative apostolic foundation of the church. Both aspects of the biblical pattern must be held together."

"The Proverbs 31 woman's celebration in the Hebrew canon — a poem used by Jewish husbands to honor their wives at the Sabbath table — is the canon's own tribute to the fullness of feminine vocation: commercial, domestic, charitable, instructional, and godly, all within the covenant household and all conducted “in the fear of the LORD” (Prov 31:30)."
